newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's once-cosseted scientists plead poverty.
newsitem.headline: Russia's once-cosseted scientists plead poverty.

text.p: Russian scientists, a privileged and respected elite in the old Soviet Union, made a desperate appeal for money on Thursday and said the country faced disaster without more government support for science.

About 600 people, waving banners that read "Without Science Russia is on the Road to Nowhere" and "Scientists -- Get Up Off Your Knees", gathered in central Moscow to cheer a succession of scientists protesting against the lack of funds.

"The funding of Russian science has shrunk fifteen-fold over the past five years. We must mobilise to halt the destruction of science," said Vladimir Strakhov, director of the Institute of Earth Sciences, who has been on hunger strike over the issue.
"We're fighting not for ourselves or this or that institute but for the whole legacy of Russian science," said the frail 64-year-old, who has been refusing food for 10 days.
Parliament will debate the government's austere 1997 budget on Friday. The opposition-dominated lower house is almost certain to reject the package at its first reading.

Viktor Kalinushkin, a top official in the Union of Workers of the Academy of Sciences, said half the country's academic institutes would have to close down within three to four months if the government did not cough up more money.
"The economic situation in the Academy has got very much worse," he added.
The Academy of Sciences, a sprawling communist-era organisation of world renown, has seen its once generous state budgets shrivel since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Many of its researchers, who span virtually all scientific disciplines, have joined the "brain drain" of talent seeking lucrative jobs in the West.
Around three quarters of the scientists who remain top up their meagre salaries with outside work.

The protesters said the government had failed even to pay the reduced funds allocated to the Academy in this year's budget and demanded a swift end to the big backlog in unpaid wages and salaries -- a problem familiar to many other Russian workers.
Groups from miners to teachers and Russia's cultural elite have staged similar protests over unpaid wages and subsidies.

Engineer Viktor Yakovlevich told Reuters he and his colleagues received their salaries only irregularly. His young assistant received only $50 a month -- an insignificant sum in the brash new capitalist Russia of free market prices.
"Wages are only half of the equation," union official Tatyana Roslyankova said. "We need funds just to keep the institutes running, let alone to press on with research."
"There is no money for heating and electricity in many institutes in Siberia and the far north, for example, where winter has already started," she said.
Roslyanokova put the average salary of Russian scientists working at the Academy at around 400,000 roubles ($80) a month.
"Science is dying in my country," said an elderly astronomer. "(President Boris) Yeltsin wants to destroy Russian science and he is being paid by Western governments to do it."
"I'm no communist but at least Stalin took science seriously and gave it the resources it needed to develop," he said.
But not all the protesters shared his view of a rosier past.

"We cannot go back to the era of indiscriminate state subsidies for science," said Anatoly Shabad, a liberal politician. "At that time too many people worked in the scientific field and not all of them deserved to be there."
For all its brilliant scientists and prestigious research centres, the Soviet Union devoted the greater part of its resources to military projects.
